scenario: AITA for leaving to see my GF when my sister told me not to when she was "in charge"? | My mom is gone for a class thing in another state, and my dad is on a business trip so its just me, my sister and my brother all alone in the house. My sister is 18, I am 17 and my brother is 12, I don't know why but my parents still felt the need to leave my sister "in charge" while they were both gone. My sister lets the power go to her head and while she can generally make my little brother obey her she has a tougher time with me. On Sunday I was gonna go out with my GF for dinner, and my sister stopped me saying that I can't leave. When asked its cause "she said so", I laughed at that and I thought she was joking but she just kept looking and I knew it was a joke. I told her she can boss (little brother's name) around but she can't boss me, and I went out with my GF. I guess my younger brother heard all the commotion and called mom saying we were "fighting" and when I came home and my mom called me she said that I'm grounded and have to dow what my sister says cause she's "in charge". I protested as best as I could but she wasn't having it and grounded me for disobeying my sister who is a pseudo parent while they are away. I just dropped it cause its not worth arguing any point with my mom. AITA here? EDIT:My brother told me afterwards that he was the one that told mom, I forgave him cause I mean I can't be mad at that little turd for too long

Thanksgiving is next week and I'm responsible for preparing the turkey for the first time. My family has a specific recipe for it that everyone expects. How would you approach that?

Preparing your family’s Thanksgiving turkey for the first time can feel daunting, but with a structured approach, you can ensure success while staying true to tradition. Here’s a step-by-step guide to help you navigate the process with confidence: --- ### **1. Review the Recipe Thoroughly** - **Clarify details**: Ask a family member to confirm the exact recipe (e.g., brining method, seasoning, cooking time, temperature, and any special techniques like butter basting or herb stuffing). - **Check for notes**: Look for handwritten instructions, family traditions (e.g., "always add a splash of bourbon" or "let it rest for 30 minutes"), or adjustments (e.g., "reduce salt if using salted butter"). - **Gather tools**: Ensure you have all necessary equipment (meat thermometer, roasting pan, basting brush, etc.). --- ### **2. Plan Ahead (Critical for First-Timers!)** - **Buy the turkey early**: Fresh turkeys sell out quickly. Opt for a **whole turkey (12–14 lbs for 6–8 people)** or a **brined turkey (10–12 lbs)** if your recipe includes brining. Frozen turkeys require more thawing time (about 24 hours per 4–5 lbs in the fridge). - **Thawing**: If frozen, thaw in the fridge (not on the counter) starting **3–4 days before cooking**. Use the "day-by-day" thawing guide: - **Day 1**: Start thawing (e.g., a 12-lb turkey needs ~3 days). - **Day 2–3**: Continue thawing; check for ice buildup. - **Day before cooking**: Ensure it’s fully thawed (liquid should run clear). - **Prep workspace**: Clean and organize your kitchen, tools, and ingredients the day before. --- ### **3. Follow the Recipe Step-by-Step** Here’s a general framework based on common family recipes (adjust for specifics): #### **A. Brining (If Applicable)** - **Why**: Brining (soaking in saltwater) keeps the turkey juicy. If your recipe includes this, start **24–48 hours before cooking**. - **How**: - Dissolve **1 cup salt + ¼ cup sugar** per gallon of water (or use a pre-made brine). - Add **aromatics** (e.g., garlic, herbs, citrus peels) if the recipe specifies. - Submerge the turkey in a **large container** (use a weight to keep it submerged). - **Rinse before cooking** and pat dry. #### **B. Pre-Cooking Prep** - **Dry the turkey thoroughly**: Pat it dry with paper towels to ensure even browning. - **Seasoning**: - **Inside cavity**: Rub with butter, herbs (thyme, rosemary, sage), garlic, and salt/pepper as per the recipe. - **Outside**: Season generously with salt, pepper, and any other spices (e.g., sage, black peppercorn). - **Stuffing (if used)**: - Prepare stuffing **ahead** (day before) and refrigerate. - Stuff loosely into the cavity (overstuffing can dry it out). Some families prefer **separate stuffing** baked in a dish. #### **C. Roasting** - **Oven setup**: - Preheat oven to **325°F (165°C)**—lower temps ensure even cooking. - Place turkey **breast-side up** on a rack in a roasting pan (for airflow). - Add **liquid** (water, broth, or apple juice) to the pan to prevent drying. - **Basting**: - Baste every **45–60 minutes** with pan juices or melted butter/herb mixture (if the recipe calls for it). - **Butter basting**: Melt butter with herbs, spoon over turkey periodically. - **Cooking time**: - **Unbrined turkey**: ~13–15 minutes per pound (e.g., 12 lbs = ~2 hours). - **Brined turkey**: ~10–12 minutes per pound (e.g., 10 lbs = ~2 hours). - **Estimated total time**: 3–4 hours (including rest time). - **Thermometer check**: - Insert a **meat thermometer** into the thickest part of the thigh (avoid bone). - **Safe temp**: **165°F (74°C)** in the thickest part of the thigh and breast. - **Don’t overcook**: Turkeys continue cooking while resting (see below). #### **D. Resting (Non-Negotiable!)** - **Why**: Letting the turkey rest redistributes juices for moist meat. - **How**: - Tent loosely with foil and let rest **30–45 minutes** before carving. - Keep warm in the oven (turn off heat) or on a warming tray. --- ### **4. Carving and Serving** - **Carve at the table**: Use a sharp knife to slice against the grain. - **Serve with pan juices**: Strain and reduce juices for gravy if your recipe includes it. - **Leftovers**: Store in airtight containers (e.g., turkey, stuffing, gravy) within 2 hours of cooking. --- ### **5. Troubleshooting Common Issues** | **Problem** | **Solution** | |---------------------------|-----------------------------------------------| | Turkey dries out | Brine it, baste often, or use a meat thermometer. | | Skin doesn’t brown | Broil for 2–3 minutes at the end (watch closely!). | | Stuffing gets soggy | Bake stuffing separately or stuff loosely. | | Overcooked | Remove from oven at 155°F (thigh) and rest. | | Turkey too salty | Rinse before cooking if brining; use unsalted butter. | --- ### **6. Pro Tips for First-Timers** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to help with basting or carving. - **Set reminders**: Use phone alarms for basting intervals and thermometer checks. - **Document**: Take photos of each step to compare with the recipe later. - **Stay calm**: If something goes wrong (e.g., oven temp fluctuates), focus on the thermometer, not the clock. --- ### **7. Family-Specific Adjustments** If your family’s recipe includes unique elements (e.g.,: - **Herb butter**: Melt butter with herbs and rub under the skin. - **Apple cider brine**: Use apple cider instead of water for a subtle sweetness. - **Dry-brine**: Salt the turkey 1–2 days before cooking (no liquid brine). - **Herb stuffing**: Use a mix of celery, onions, breadcrumbs, and herbs. ), double-check these details with a family member. --- ### **8. Timeline Example (For a 12-lb Turkey)** | **Day Before** | **Morning Of** | **Cooking Day** | |--------------------------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------------| | Brine turkey (if needed) | Thaw turkey (if frozen) | Preheat oven to 325°F. | | Prep stuffing | Dry turkey, season | Place turkey in oven. | | | | Baste every 45 mins. | | | | Check temp at ~1.5 hours (155°F). | | | | Rest 30–45 mins before carving. | --- ### **Final Encouragement** You’ve got this! The key is to **follow the recipe closely**, **use a thermometer**, and **let the turkey rest**. Even if it’s not perfect, the love and effort will shine through. If you’re unsure about any step, don’t hesitate to ask for help—family traditions are meant to be shared. prediction.raw: This scenario is a complex mix of **power dynamics, sibling rivalry, and parental expectations**, and whether you were "AITA" depends on how you weigh **personal autonomy, respect for authority, and the context of your family’s situation**. Here’s my breakdown: --- ### **Why This Situation Is Complicated** 1. **Unfair Authority**: - Your sister was **not actually in charge**—she was given a role that didn’t align with her age or maturity level (especially since she struggles to enforce rules with you). This is a **parental oversight**, not a legitimate authority figure. If your parents had been home, they would’ve handled it differently. **You weren’t disobeying a real authority; you were pushing back against an arbitrary power grab.** 2. **Your Sister’s Hypocrisy**: - She can control your brother but not you? That’s **inconsistent and unfair**. If she’s the "parent" in this scenario, she should treat everyone equally—or admit she’s not capable. Your response ("she can’t boss me") was **logical and reasonable** in that moment. 3. **Your Brother’s Role**: - He’s **12**, not a reliable mediator. His decision to call your mom (even if he exaggerated) was **childish and manipulative**. While you forgave him, his actions **escalated the conflict unnecessarily**. That said, he’s still young, so cut him some slack. 4. **Your Mom’s Reaction**: - She **sided with your sister’s arbitrary rule** without questioning why or how it was enforced. This suggests she **doesn’t trust you to handle responsibility** (even though you’re 17) and **favors your sister’s perceived authority**. This is **unfair to you** and reinforces a power imbalance. --- ### **Was It Wrong to Leave?** **No, it wasn’t wrong—but it was risky.** - **Ethically**: You weren’t breaking any *real* rules. Your sister wasn’t a parent; she was **abusing a temporary role** to control you. Your mom’s grounding was **retaliation**, not a fair consequence. - **Pragmatically**: You could’ve handled it better: - **Option 1 (Better)**: Tell your sister, *"I respect that you’re trying to help, but I need to go out with my GF. If Mom asks, I’ll tell her you were just trying to keep us safe."* Then leave. This **acknowledges her effort** while setting a boundary. - **Option 2 (Your Choice)**: You **called her out**, which was bold but might’ve escalated things. Since your brother was there to rat you out, you were **outnumbered**. - **Long-term**: If you keep pushing back like this, your mom might **double down on controlling you** (e.g., more grounding, less trust). But if you **stand your ground**, she might eventually see you as a **responsible adult** rather than a child to be managed. --- ### **Was It Wrong to Laugh at Your Sister?** **Yes, but not maliciously.** - Laughing when she said *"she said so"* was **mocking her authority**, which could’ve been seen as **disrespectful** in that moment. Even if she was joking, it **escalated tension** before it needed to. - A better approach: *"Yeah, I know, but I’m not letting you control me like that."* (Still firm, but less confrontational.) --- ### **Was It Wrong to Not Argue with Your Mom?** **Yes, but understandable.** - **Protested as best you could**: That’s smart. Arguing with your mom when she’s already decided might’ve made things worse. - **But**: If you **complied without a fight**, you’re teaching her that **she can override your boundaries**. Next time, she might expect you to **always defer to your sister**—even when it’s unfair. - **Future strategy**: When she grounds you, say: *"I get that you’re worried, but I’m 17. If you’re not here, I should have a say in my own life. Can we talk about this when you’re back?"* This **shifts the conversation to fairness** rather than defiance. --- ### **Score: 0.5/1 (Neither Fully Right Nor Wrong)** - **Why not 1 (fully right)?** - You **didn’t respect your sister’s temporary role** (even if it was unfair). - You **could’ve handled the escalation better** (e.g., not laughing, not leaving without a clear boundary-setting). - **Why not 0 (fully wrong)?** - You **weren’t disobeying a real authority**—your sister wasn’t a parent. - Your mom’s punishment was **unfair and arbitrary**, not a legitimate consequence. - You **stood up for yourself**, which is healthy, even if the execution wasn’t perfect. --- ### **How to Fix This Moving Forward** 1. **Set Boundaries with Your Sister**: - Next time she tries to control you, say: *"I respect that you’re trying to help, but I’m not a kid. If Mom asks, I’ll tell her you were just looking out for us."* This **limits her power** without being confrontational. 2. **Talk to Your Mom (When She’s Calm)**: - Frame it as: *"I know you trust [Sister] to help, but I’m 17. Can we agree that when you’re not here, I should have more say in my own life?"* - If she refuses, **comply but don’t accept it as permanent**. Keep testing limits (e.g., *"Can I stay out later this weekend?"*) to see where she draws the line. 3. **Protect Your Relationship with Your GF**: - If your mom keeps grounding you for this, **have a backup plan** (e.g., meet her somewhere else if she can’t come to your house). 4. **Don’t Let Your Brother Manipulate You**: - Next time he rats you out, **call him out gently**: *"Dude, I know you’re mad, but calling Mom isn’t cool. We’re a team."* (Then forgive him—kids are kids.) --- ### **Final Verdict** You were **not wrong for leaving**, but you **could’ve handled the power struggle more strategically**. Your mom’s reaction was **unfair**, and your sister’s authority was **flimsy at best**. The real issue here isn’t that you disobeyed—it’s that your parents **failed to set clear, fair rules** when they left. **Next time**, use **firm but respectful language** to push back against arbitrary control. Stand your ground, but do it in a way that **doesn’t give your mom ammunition** to punish you unfairly. Would you like help drafting a script for talking to your mom about this?
